articleGender.example: fromage is masculine, so the article is un.

articleGenderPredicted.template: {noun} is probably {gender}: {reason} So the article would be {article}.
articleGenderPredicted.example: influenceuse is probably feminine: words ending in -euse usually are. So the article would be une.

contractedGender.template: {noun} is {gender}, so {preposition} and its article make {article}.
contractedGender.example: maison is feminine, so à and its article make à la.

articleNumberPlural.template: {noun} is plural, so the article is {article}.
articleNumberPlural.example: montagnes is plural, so the article is les.

articleNumberSingular.hint: {article} is plural, so the noun after it is too.
articleNumberSingular.template: {article} is plural, so the noun after it is too: {fix}.
articleNumberSingular.example: des is plural, so the noun after it is too: des pommes.

contraction.example: à + le always contracts to au.

agreementGender.hint: The adjective must agree with {noun}, which is {gender}.
agreementGender.template: The adjective must agree with {noun}, which is {gender}.
agreementGender.example: The adjective must agree with maison, which is feminine.

agreementNumber.hint: The adjective must agree with {noun}, which is {number}.
agreementNumber.template: The adjective must agree with {noun}, which is {number}.
agreementNumber.example: The adjective must agree with pommes, which is plural.

agreementGenderAndNumber.hint: The adjective must agree with {noun}, which is {gender} and {number}.
agreementGenderAndNumber.template: The adjective must agree with {noun}, which is {gender} and {number}.
agreementGenderAndNumber.example: The adjective must agree with tables, which is feminine and plural.

spelling.hint: {word} isn't in the French dictionary, but a word close to it is. Look again at {where}.
spelling.template: {word} isn't in the French dictionary. Did you mean {suggestion}?
spelling.example: gentile isn't in the French dictionary. Did you mean gentille?

unknownWord.template: {word} isn't in the French dictionary, and there's no close match to suggest.
unknownWord.example: Ahdourdui isn't in the French dictionary, and there's no close match to suggest.

runTogether.hint: {word} reads as two words run together. Look for where the space or apostrophe goes.
runTogether.example: mecouche is two words run together: me couche.

enArticle.hint: En doesn't normally come before le, la or les.
enArticle.template: En doesn't normally come before le, la or les. It should be {fix}.
enArticle.example: En doesn't normally come before le, la or les. It should be dans les.

lookAlike.example: cava is a past form of caver, “to dig,” as in il cava un trou. It should be ça va.

wordChoice.example: French says avoir for hunger, thirst, fear and sleepiness. It should be j'ai faim.

negation.hint: In writing, “no longer” needs both ne and plus. Without ne, this reads as “more.”
negation.template: In writing, “no longer” is ne… plus: {corrected}. Without ne, this reads as “more.”
negation.example: In writing, “no longer” is ne… plus: il ne dort plus. Without ne, this reads as “more.”

negativeArticle.hint: After a negative such as pas, jamais or plus, {article} usually becomes de.
negativeArticle.template: After {negation}, {article} becomes de, or d' before a vowel: {fix}. Être is the exception: ce n'est pas du pain.
negativeArticle.example: After pas, du becomes de, or d' before a vowel: de pain. Être is the exception: ce n'est pas du pain.

accentAfterVerb.hint: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't follow another verb like {verb}.
accentAfterVerb.template: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't follow another verb like {verb}. Here it's the preposition à.
accentAfterVerb.example: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't follow another verb like vais. Here it's the preposition à.

accentAfterJusqu.hint: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which never follows jusqu'.
accentAfterJusqu.template: a without an accent is the verb avoir. After jusqu', it's always the preposition à.
accentAfterJusqu.example: a without an accent is the verb avoir. After jusqu', it's always the preposition à.

accentAfterDans.hint: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't follow dans.
accentAfterDans.template: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't follow dans. The preposition is à, and it takes the place of dans.
accentAfterDans.example: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't follow dans. The preposition is à, and it takes the place of dans.

accentAfterAdjective.hint: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't join an adjective like {adjective} to an infinitive.
accentAfterAdjective.template: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't join an adjective like {adjective} to an infinitive. Here it's the preposition à.
accentAfterAdjective.example: a without an accent is the verb avoir, which can't join an adjective like facile to an infinitive. Here it's the preposition à.

graveAfterSubject.hint: à with an accent is a preposition, and a preposition can't come right after the subject {subject}.
graveAfterSubject.template: à with an accent is a preposition, and a preposition can't come right after the subject {subject}. Here it's the verb avoir: a, with no accent.
graveAfterSubject.example: à with an accent is a preposition, and a preposition can't come right after the subject il. Here it's the verb avoir: a, with no accent.

graveInIlYA.hint: In il y a, the a is the verb avoir.
graveInIlYA.template: In il y a, the a is the verb avoir, so it has no accent.
graveInIlYA.example: In il y a, the a is the verb avoir, so it has no accent.

auxiliaryChoice.hint: {verb} takes être in the past, not avoir.
auxiliaryChoice.template: {verb} takes être in the past, not avoir: {fix}.
auxiliaryChoice.example: aller takes être in the past, not avoir: je suis allé.

participleWithAvoir.hint: With avoir, the past participle doesn't change to match the subject.
participleWithAvoir.template: With avoir, the past participle doesn't change to match the subject, so it stays {fix}.
participleWithAvoir.example: With avoir, the past participle doesn't change to match the subject, so it stays mangé.

participleWithEtre.hint: With être, the past participle agrees with {subject}.
participleWithEtre.template: With être, the past participle agrees with {subject}, so it's {fix}.
participleWithEtre.example: With être, the past participle agrees with elles, so it's allées.

generalArticle.hint: After {verb}, a noun for something in general takes le, la or les.
generalArticle.template: After {verb}, a noun for something in general takes le, la or les: {fix}.
generalArticle.example: After aimer, a noun for something in general takes le, la or les: le fromage.

subjectVerb.example: With je, aller takes the form vais.

nearFutureInfinitive.hint: After aller, the next verb stays in the infinitive.
nearFutureInfinitive.template: After aller, the next verb stays in the infinitive: {fix}.
nearFutureInfinitive.example: After aller, the next verb stays in the infinitive: pleuvoir.

siClause.hint: After si meaning if, French doesn't use the future or the conditional.
siClause.template: After si meaning if, French uses the {tense} instead: {fix}.
siClause.example: After si meaning if, French uses the present instead: viens.

siClauseResult.hint: With si + {tense}, the other half of the sentence uses the {other}.
siClauseResult.template: With si + {tense}, the other half of the sentence uses the {other}: {fix}.
siClauseResult.example: With si + imperfect, the other half of the sentence uses the conditional: achèterais.

futureAfterQuand.hint: When the action is still to come, French uses the future after {trigger}.
futureAfterQuand.template: When the action is still to come, French uses the future after {trigger}: {fix}.
futureAfterQuand.example: When the action is still to come, French uses the future after quand: arriverai.

subjunctive.example: After il faut que, French uses the subjunctive: fasse.

objectPronounDirect.hint: {verb} takes a direct object: le, la or les.
objectPronounDirect.template: {verb} takes a direct object: le, la or les. Here: {fix}.
objectPronounDirect.example: Voir takes a direct object: le, la or les. Here: l'.

objectPronounIndirect.hint: {verb} takes à + a person: lui or leur.
objectPronounIndirect.template: {verb} takes à + a person: lui or leur. Here: {fix}.
objectPronounIndirect.example: Téléphoner takes à + a person: lui or leur. Here: lui.

relativeQue.hint: Here {subject} is the subject, so the relative pronoun can't be qui.
relativeQue.template: Here {subject} is the subject, so the relative pronoun is que.
relativeQue.example: Here je is the subject, so the relative pronoun is que.

relativeDont.hint: French says {phrase} de something, so que doesn't fit here.
relativeDont.template: French says {phrase} de something, so the relative pronoun is dont.
relativeDont.example: French says avoir besoin de something, so the relative pronoun is dont.

etOrEst.hint: Et means and; est means is. Which one does this sentence need?
etOrEst.template: Et means and; est means is. This sentence needs {fix}.
etOrEst.example: Et means and; est means is. This sentence needs est.

meaning.hint: Both are correct French, but they mean different things. {note}
meaning.template: Both are correct French, but they mean different things. {note}
meaning.example: Both are correct French, but they mean different things. Pas encore means not yet; ne… plus means no longer.

idiom.hint: This is correct, but a native would usually say it another way. {note}
idiom.template: This is correct. Here's how a native would usually say it: {suggestion}. {note}
idiom.example: This is correct. Here's how a native would usually say it: a du sens. Faire du sens copies the English “make sense”; French usually says avoir du sens.

preposition.example: Dépendre takes de before what it's about. It should be dépend de.

placePreposition.example: Canada is a masculine country, so French says au Canada.

elision.hint: Before a vowel sound, {word} drops its last letter.
elision.template: Before a vowel sound, {word} drops its last letter and takes an apostrophe: {fix}.
elision.example: Before a vowel sound, je drops its last letter and takes an apostrophe: j'aime.

elisionContraction.template: {word} only comes before a consonant. Before a vowel sound, French writes {fix}.
elisionContraction.example: au only comes before a consonant. Before a vowel sound, French writes à l'école.

possessiveGender.example: mère is feminine, so the possessive is ma mère.

possessiveBeforeVowel.hint: Before a vowel sound, ma, ta and sa change form.
possessiveBeforeVowel.template: Before a vowel sound, ma, ta and sa become mon, ton and son, even for a feminine noun: {fix}.
possessiveBeforeVowel.example: Before a vowel sound, ma, ta and sa become mon, ton and son, even for a feminine noun: mon amie.

reflexiveAuxiliary.hint: A reflexive verb, with se, takes a different helper verb in the past.
reflexiveAuxiliary.template: A reflexive verb, with se, always takes être in the past: {fix}.
reflexiveAuxiliary.example: A reflexive verb, with se, always takes être in the past: il s'est trompé.

sentenceCapital.hint: Look at how this sentence starts.
sentenceCapital.template: A sentence starts with a capital letter: {fix}.
sentenceCapital.example: A sentence starts with a capital letter: Il.

lowercaseDayOrMonth.hint: French writes days and months differently from English.
lowercaseDayOrMonth.template: In French, days of the week and months take no capital letter: {fix}.
lowercaseDayOrMonth.example: In French, days of the week and months take no capital letter: lundi.

lowercaseLanguage.hint: French writes the names of languages differently from English.
lowercaseLanguage.template: In French, the name of a language takes no capital letter: {fix}. Only the people take one, as in les Français.
lowercaseLanguage.example: In French, the name of a language takes no capital letter: anglais. Only the people take one, as in les Français.

lowercaseNationality.hint: {word} describes someone here rather than naming a people.
lowercaseNationality.template: {word} describes someone here, so it takes no capital letter: {fix}. Only the noun for the people takes one, as in les Américains.
lowercaseNationality.example: Américain describes someone here, so it takes no capital letter: américain. Only the noun for the people takes one, as in les Américains.

lowercaseJe.hint: Je isn't written like the English I.
lowercaseJe.template: Unlike the English I, je takes a capital letter only at the start of a sentence: {fix}.
lowercaseJe.example: Unlike the English I, je takes a capital letter only at the start of a sentence: je.
